what_it_does: Boolean satisfiability — the problem of figuring out whether any combination of true/false variable assignments can make a logical formula evaluate to true — is one of the most important hard problems in computer science, used in chip verification, AI planning, and cryptography. The challenge is that SAT problems come in wildly different shapes: some are small but fiendishly complex, others are huge but have exploitable structure, and no single solving algorithm works best for all of them. This paper presents Chameleon-SAT, a custom chip (an ASIC — a silicon chip designed for one specific task) that does the math for SAT solving directly inside its memory arrays using a mix of analog and digital circuits, which avoids the bottleneck of constantly shuttling data between separate memory and logic chips. The chip can switch between three different solving strategies — local search (randomly flipping variables and checking if the formula gets closer to satisfied), DPLL (a systematic tree-search that tries assignments one by one), and CDCL (a smarter tree-search that remembers which variable combinations caused failures and avoids repeating them) — picking the right algorithm based on the problem at hand.
